item.text: The reconnaissance establishes the core evidence environment: a highly visible international war with strong external monitoring abroad, but sharply constrained domestic reporting after March 2022. I’m now filtering opened sources into reusable, source-profiled claims and keeping country indicators explicitly separate from ruler-attributed conduct.

Evidence-collection pass completed; no scores or score ranges assigned.

The supplied local package was used first. I retained local facts as structured context, not automatic ruler evidence. Key local anchors include 2022 political deterioration (LF1405, LF1411–LF1419), military spending/conflict exposure (LF126–LF129, LF243–LF246), aggregate welfare/economic outcomes (LF1631–LF1637, LF2151–LF2159), corruption context (LF2276–LF2279), and effectiveness context (LF2326–LF2327). LF532’s warning was preserved: government-actor killings do not establish Putin’s personal direction.

The internet ledger yielded 19 provisional evidence items:

- E001: Kremlin formal presidential policy and Supreme Commander authority.
- E002–E004: UN documentation of Russia’s armed attack, civilian harm, summary executions, lack of Russian investigations, and General Assembly condemnation. [UN HRMMU](https://ukraine.ohchr.org/en/175994-update-human-rights-situation-ukraine-EN), [UN executions report](https://ukraine.ohchr.org/en/UN-report-details-summary-executions-of-civilians-by-Russian-troops-from-February-to-April), [UNGA resolution coverage](https://press.un.org/en/2022/ga12407.doc.htm)
- E005–E007: nuclear-alert reporting, UN de-escalation warnings, and ZNPP safety-risk evidence. The IAEA item is discovery-only because the source returned HTTP 402 and lacked a retrievable precise locator. [UN nuclear-alert statement](https://www.un.org/sg/en/content/sg/statements/2022-02-28/secretary-generals-remarks-the-general-assembly-emergency-special-session-ukraine-delivered), [UN de-escalation statement](https://www.un.org/sg/en/content/sg/press-encounter/2022-03-28/secretary-generals-press-encounter-the-war-ukraine)
- E008–E010: Putin-signed censorship laws, anti-war protest prosecutions, journalist flight, and mass detentions. [HRW censorship report](https://www.hrw.org/news/2022/03/07/russia-criminalizes-independent-war-reporting-anti-war-protests), [HRW protest detentions](https://www.hrw.org/news/2022/02/26/russia-arbitrary-detentions-anti-war-protesters)
- E011–E012: IMF and World Bank assessments of sanctions, recession, stabilization measures, inflation, and investment/consumption shocks. [IMF report](https://www.imf.org/-/media/Files/Publications/REO/EUR/2022/April/English/text.ashx), [World Bank assessment](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2022/04/10/russian-invasion-to-shrink-ukraine-economy-by-45-percent)
- E013–E014: official 2022 health/education agenda and Putin’s family-support decree.
- E015–E016: contested OCCRP/ICIJ allegations concerning Putin-linked wealth networks and the alleged palace; both retain denials and remain context-only. [OCCRP banking investigation](https://www.occrp.org/en/project/the-panama-papers/russia-banking-on-influence), [OCCRP palace report](https://www.occrp.org/en/news/navalny-hits-back-by-exposing-putins-fairytale-palace)
- E017–E018: Putin’s September partial mobilization and September annexation-treaty acts.
- E019: Putin’s stated historical-unity program concerning Ukraine.

Chapter yield:

- 1B: strongest on alerting, rhetoric, crisis risk, and inherited arsenal exposure; major gaps remain on command safety, arms control, proliferation, expertise, and dual-use risk.
- 2B: strongest chapter yield. Direct evidence covers initiation, civilian harm, legality, accountability, mobilization, annexation, and peace alternatives. Proxy control and internal deliberation remain gaps.
- 3B: strong evidence for protest detention, censorship, physical-integrity harm abroad, and weak remedy; domestic prison, torture, vulnerable-group, and incitement evidence remains incomplete.
- 4B: extensive local political-freedom context plus direct target-year censorship and protest evidence. Gaps include target-year transfer/election evidence, courts, local autonomy, minorities, and digital surveillance.
- 5B: local outcomes plus IMF/World Bank shock and stabilization evidence. Gaps include appointments, market rules, capture, distribution, implementation audits, and correction.
- 6B: strong aggregate health/education outcomes but weak ruler-attributed delivery and equity evidence; official policy records are context rather than independent effectiveness proof.
- 7B: insufficient personal-nexus evidence. National corruption indicators were not personalized. OCCRP items remain allegations/context only.
- 8B: partial authority/program/action chain through formal presidential authority, mobilization, annexation, stated ideology, and macro-stabilization measures. Gaps remain on portfolio breadth, personnel, adaptation, independent outcomes, and durability.

Bias findings: international reporting is unusually abundant, while domestic reporting after March 2022 was constrained; war and censorship dominate the source pool; complaint volume is therefore not comparable across periods; population denominator is supplied as 144,236,933; inherited conditions and external sanctions are separated from ruler-attributed acts.
